the fluorescence of dye-saturated montmorillonite is enhanced by several order of magnitude in reduced charge montmorilltonites.
fluorescence intensity of montmorillonite-methylene blue complexes can be increased by several orders of magnitudes by reducing the charge density of the host and by controlling the dye adsorption.
fluorescence of MB-RCM is enhanced by several order of magnitude with respect in comparison to MB-SWy and MB-SAz.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fluorescence of dye-montmorillonite complexes, and it is focused on the influence of the charge reduction of montmorillonite on the intensity and the position of the emission spectra of MB-RCM.
the preparation of a novel type of dye-loaded RCMs, which are characterized by high fluorescence intensity and are suitable as solid state fluorimetric probes.
the preparation, characterization, and fluorescence properties of low-loaded MB-montmorillonites complexes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed fluorescence is not due to dye aggregates but to the isolated dye molecules.
RCMs can be used to enhance fluorescence intensity of dye adsorption on the surface of montmorillonite.
the fluorescence of MB-RCM composites depends strongly on the adsorption degree of MB on RCM and the nature of MB species in the solid state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fluorescence of dye-montmorillonite complexes is strongly dependent on the dye concentration.
the fluorescence intensity of MB-RCM systems is enhanced by the decrease of the MB aggregation.
the intensity of fluorescence of dye-loaded montmorillonites can be controlled by fine tuning of the dye adsorption degree.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the intensity of dye fluorescence can be significantly increased by controlling the dye adsorption degree in RCM.
RCMs can be used as an efficient tool to produce solid-state dye aggregates with a desired size and shape.
fluorescence intensity is enhanced by several factors: (1) the absence of aggregates, (2) the absence of quenching centers, and (3) the absence of energy transfer between dye molecules.
